hints: Look carefully at the diagram and notice which two gas streams pass through the heat exchanger in opposite directions.
Remember the converter runs hot at about 450 C, so the gases leaving it are very hot while the incoming $\text{N}_2 + \text{H}_2$ mixture is relatively cool.
Think about what warming the incoming gases does to the rate of reaction, and whether heating changes the position of equilibrium for this exothermic reaction.
walkthrough:
**Follow the gas flows in the diagram**

Look at the arrows. Cool incoming $\text{N}_2 + \text{H}_2$ goes one way through the heat exchanger toward the catalytic converter.

Hot product gases from the converter go the opposite way through the same exchanger toward the condenser. So heat passes from hot to cold.

**Recall the Haber conditions**

The key reaction is:
$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g) \quad \Delta H < 0$$
It needs an iron catalyst at about 450 C and high pressure to go fast enough. Cold gases entering would cool the catalyst and slow the reaction.

**Decide warming or cooling, rate or equilibrium**

The heat exchanger uses waste heat from the products to pre-warm the reactants. This saves energy and keeps the converter hot.

Warming does not shift this exothermic equilibrium to make more $\text{NH}_3$. It simply gives particles more kinetic energy, so more successful collisions per second and a faster reaction.

options.A: Incorrect. The incoming mixture needs warming, not cooling. The converter must stay hot (around 450 C) for the iron catalyst to work effectively, and cooling would slow the reaction down.
options.B: Incorrect. This describes the job of the condenser, not the heat exchanger. The condenser cools the product mixture so $\text{NH}_3$ liquefies and can be removed, leaving unused $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$ to be recycled.
options.C: Incorrect. Warming is right, but the reason is wrong. The forward reaction is exothermic, so warming actually shifts equilibrium to the left, giving less $\text{NH}_3$ at equilibrium. The high temperature is used for speed, not for yield.
options.D: Correct. The hot gases leaving the catalytic converter pre-heat the cool incoming $\text{N}_2 + \text{H}_2$ in the heat exchanger. This brings reactants up to operating temperature quickly and economically, so they react faster in the converter.
